lessons.title: Build and run a Go program
lessons.summary: You edit main.go but run the previously built executable without rebuilding. What can appear?
explanation: An executable program uses package main and a main function. Imports name packages whose exported operations the code uses, such as fmt.Println.
go build translates the program into an executable. go run also builds before running; it is not an interpreter reading source statement by statement.
Editing main.go does not change an executable already built from an earlier version.
This course uses official Go 1.27.3. In the shared environment /usr/bin/go is an unrelated game, so validation uses the approved workspace-local compiler path.
Expected output or behavior: Ready. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: In a new folder save main.go. Use the installed Go toolchain to run go build -o lesson main.go, then ./lesson. Compare an edited source before and after rebuilding. You may trace it without a Go compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.

lessons.title: Types and constant inference
lessons.summary: Change 5 to 5.0 in the short declaration. What prints?
explanation: count := 3 declares a variable whose inferred type is int. Type inference does not make its type change on each assignment.
int is either 32 or 64 bits depending on the implementation. int64 explicitly selects a signed 64-bit type; float64 represents approximate fractional values.
A constant such as 3 can be used where a compatible numeric type is expected if its value fits. A typed numeric variable follows stricter assignment rules.
Two integer operands produce an integer result. A floating-point operand can make this division floating-point.
Expected output or behavior: 2. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Compare integer and floating operands, then inspect why the result type differs without assuming int is always 32 bits. You may trace it without a Go compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.

lessons.title: Explicit numeric conversion
lessons.summary: Change value to 3.9. What prints?
explanation: int(value) converts a numeric value to int. It does not parse a String; text parsing belongs to functions such as strconv.Atoi.
For an ordinary in-range float64 value, conversion to int discards its fractional part toward zero rather than rounding to nearest.
A conversion is not proof that an external value is sensible or safely representable. Avoid relying on out-of-range conversion results.
A non-integer constant cannot be converted to an integer type unless representable as that type. This example deliberately converts a runtime float64 variable.
Expected output or behavior: -3. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Compare small positive and negative fractional variables. Do not confuse numeric conversion with parsing text. You may trace it without a Go compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.

lessons.title: Zero values and initialization
lessons.summary: Assign count=4 before printing. What prints?
explanation: var count int starts at 0. bool starts false and string starts empty. This gives a defined initial state rather than uninitialized local data.
Arrays and structs have recursively zero-valued elements or fields. Some reference-like types have nil zero values and require care before mutation.
A zero-valued quantity may still violate a business rule; language initialization does not validate meaning.
A later assignment changes that variable from its zero value to the assigned one.
Expected output or behavior: 0. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Compare zero values of int,bool,and string, then consider which are acceptable in a small task. You may trace it without a Go compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.

lessons.title: Boolean conditions and short-circuiting
lessons.summary: Set denominator to 0. What prints?
explanation: Go if conditions use bool expressions. Integers and strings are not automatically treated as true or false.
&& skips its right operand when the left is false. || skips the right operand when the left is true.
denominator !=0 comes first. When it is false, the division is not evaluated.
Short-circuiting controls evaluation as well as the final truth value.
Expected output or behavior: true. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Strings bytes and runes
lessons.summary: Change the text to "A". What prints?
explanation: len(text) counts bytes, not necessarily Unicode characters. UTF-8 encodes many non-ASCII code points using multiple bytes.
rune is an alias for int32. The conversion []rune(text) decodes UTF-8 into runes; len of that slice counts code points, not user-perceived grapheme clusters.
byte is an alias for uint8. Indexing a String returns a byte; ranging over text decodes runes.
The UTF-8 source literal é occupies two bytes and one Unicode code point. ASCII A occupies one byte and one code point.
Expected output or behavior: 2 1. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Formatting values deliberately
lessons.summary: Change the format from %q to %s. What prints?
explanation: fmt.Printf uses a format string. %d formats an integer in decimal; %q formats a quoted escaped representation for a String. %s prints String content without surrounding quotation marks.
The escape \n adds a newline. fmt.Println adds its own line ending and spaces between separate arguments.
Displaying a value as text does not change the stored value’s type.
Use a suitable formatting verb instead of assuming every verb means the same thing. Go can report formatting mismatch text; that is not correct data output.
Expected output or behavior: "moon". Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Scope and short declarations
lessons.summary: Replace the inner := with =. What prints?
explanation: Inside a function, := is a short variable declaration. In the same block it needs at least one new non-blank name.
A new score declared inside braces is distinct from an outer score. Updating that inner object does not update the outer one.
= assigns an existing name instead of declaring a new one. Scope determines which existing variable is selected.
Similar spelling is not proof of the same object. Read the block boundaries and declaration operator.

Expected output or behavior: 7
3. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Loop control
lessons.summary: Replace continue with break. What prints?
explanation: for i:=0; i<4; i++ initializes once, tests before each body and updates after each completed body.
continue proceeds to the next iteration; the update still runs before the next test.
break stops this nearest loop instead of skipping only one pass.
This example uses a small finite range. A loop’s syntax does not by itself prove termination.

lessons.title: Array values and copying
lessons.summary: Change only the copy assignment value from 9 to 7. What prints?
explanation: [3]int is an array of exactly three ints. A different length is a different array type.
Assigning one array variable to another copies its array value. A later element assignment to the copy does not mutate the original array.
Index 0 selects the first element. A runtime out-of-range index panics; it does not grow the array.
Do not transfer the copy rule to slices or pointers without examining their semantics.
Expected output or behavior: 2 9. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Slice views and shared arrays
lessons.summary: Change view[0]=9 to view[1]=9. What does the unchanged print show?
explanation: A slice carries a reference to underlying array storage plus length and capacity. Assigning a slice copies this descriptor, not all its elements.
values[1:3] includes indices 1 and 2, excluding 3. Updating view[0] updates the underlying element at values[1].
len(view) gives the accessible length. Capacity is a separate concept used for reslicing and growth.
Changing a shared element is visible through any overlapping slice or array view.
Expected output or behavior: 9. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Append length and capacity
lessons.summary: Create the initial slice with capacity 2 instead of 1. What prints after the same append/update?
explanation: append adds values and returns a slice descriptor. Store that result because length or underlying storage may change.
make([]int,1,1) creates a slice with length 1 and capacity 1. Appending one more value requires a new backing array in this case.
An alias to the old full-capacity slice still refers to the old array after append allocates a new one.
The exact chosen new capacity is an implementation detail. This example relies only on the documented need to grow beyond capacity.

Complete local Go example; the app itself does not execute it:
```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
)

func main() {
	values := make([]int, 1, 1)
	values[0] = 3
	old := values
	values = append(values, 7)
	values[0] = 9
	fmt.Println(old[0], values[0])
}

```
Expected output or behavior: 3 9. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Compare enough capacity with forced growth. Explain sharing without predicting an undocumented capacity growth factor. You may trace it without a Go compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.

lessons.title: Copy into independent slice storage
lessons.summary: Replace the allocation and copy with target:=source. What prints after target[0]=9?
explanation: copy(dst,src) copies up to the smaller length and returns the number copied. It does not automatically grow the destination.
make([]int,len(source)) provides separate storage for the destination elements.
target := source would share backing storage. Calling copy after separate allocation copies the elements instead.
For int elements this separates the values. A slice of pointers or nested slices can still share referenced objects; this is not a universal deep copy.
Expected output or behavior: 2 9. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Maps and mutation
lessons.summary: Change the alias update to 7. What prints?
explanation: map[string]int maps String keys to int values. A map literal creates initialized map storage.
Assigning a map variable does not clone its entries. Mutating through an alias is visible through the original.
A map’s nil zero value supports reading and len, but assignment of an entry requires an initialized map, such as one made with make or a literal.
Do not depend on map iteration order for deterministic output. This example looks up a known key directly.
Expected output or behavior: 5. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.summary: Look up "rest" instead. What prints?

value,ok := counts[key] returns the value and a Boolean indicating whether the key exists.

lessons.title: Range traversal
lessons.summary: Replace value+=1 with values[i]+=1. What is the final printed slice?
explanation: for i,value := range values visits each slice element with its index and a copy of its element value.
value += 1 adds one and stores the result in value. Assigning to this local value variable does not by itself update values[i]. Use the indexed assignment to mutate the slot.
_ discards an unwanted range result. This example uses both results to make their roles visible.

lessons.title: Variadic functions
lessons.summary: Replace the call with total() and remove the now-unused values declaration. What prints?
explanation: func total(values ...int) receives the provided ints as a slice inside the function.
total(values...) supplies slice elements to the variadic parameter. The dots are part of call syntax, not a loop.
Calling total() gives no elements. The loop body runs zero times, leaving the initialized sum at 0.
Variadic calls change how many values are supplied, not the declared element type. Go rejects unused local variable declarations, so remove a local values declaration if its only use is removed.

lessons.title: Closures and captured variables
lessons.summary: Change the assignment before invocation to factor=5. What prints?
explanation: func(value int) int { ... } can be assigned to a variable and called later.
The literal refers to factor from its surrounding scope. Calling it reads that variable’s current value rather than necessarily freezing the creation-time value.
The function body runs at transform(3), after the assignment to factor.
This single-threaded example is deterministic. Capturing a variable does not make concurrent reads and writes automatically safe.
